source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of LLMs
finding: LLMs alone rarely produce executable plans in IPC-style domains. Humans on blocksworld mostly succeed and mostly find optimal plans.
numbers: Autonomous mode average success about 3%. Human baseline: 39 of 50 (78%) valid plans; 35 of 39 (89.7%) of those optimal. LLM plan plus LPG repair: average edit distance 7.22 vs final plan length 11.7.
limits: GPT-3 family and BLOOM only; old models. Small human sample (50).
agent_relevance: A fair human reference for difference-reduction planning. Raw LLM plan generation is a weak operator for O5; use LLM output only as a heuristic seed that a checker repairs.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench
finding: Blocksworld plan generation is far from solved for GPT-4. Renaming actions and objects (Mystery Blocksworld) collapses accuracy, which points to pattern matching rather than state-goal reasoning.
numbers: Plan generation (600 instances): GPT-4 206/600 (34.3%), InstructGPT-3 41/600 (6.8%). Mystery Blocksworld deceptive: GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%); randomized: 12/600 (2%).
limits: GPT-4 as of early 2023. Later reasoning models score much higher (see b03).
agent_relevance: Test O5 on obfuscated or renamed domains. A scaffold that only works on familiar surface forms is not doing difference reduction.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? (o1 on PlanBench)
finding: o1-preview solves almost all small Blocksworld but drops sharply with obfuscation and with plan length. A classical planner is perfect and far cheaper.
numbers: 600 Blocksworld (3-5 blocks): o1-preview 587/600 (97.8%), o1-mini 340/600 (56.6%), Fast Downward 600/600 in 0.265 s vs 40.43 s. Mystery BW: o1-preview 52.8%, o1-mini 19.1%. Randomized Mystery BW: o1-preview 37.3%. 110 larger problems (6-20 blocks, 20-40 steps): o1-preview 23.63%. Unsolvable instances: only 27% correctly flagged (Blocksworld), 16% (randomized mystery).
quote: Far surpassing any LLM, o1 correctly answers 97.8% of these instances.
limits: Preliminary one-week evaluation. Single provider.
agent_relevance: Plan length is the boundary: difference reduction at long horizon needs an external check. Add an unsolvable-goal exit because models rarely say 'impossible'.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Chain-of-thought helps on Blocksworld only when the demonstrated procedure matches the query class almost exactly. Gains vanish as stack size grows beyond the examples. Models do not learn a general goal-reduction procedure from demonstrations.
numbers: Table-to-stack, 261 instances, GPT-4: zero-shot 3.83%; stacking-specific CoT 59.3%; universal algorithm CoT 51.3%; progression-proof CoT 6.89%. GPT-4-Turbo: zero-shot 19.1%, stacking CoT 40.6%. Self-consistency lowered accuracy. Fast Downward 100%.
quote: contrary to previous claims in the literature, CoT's performance improvements do not stem from the model learning general algorithmic procedures
limits: GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus (2024). Blocksworld and three synthetic tasks only.
agent_relevance: Handing the agent a general 'reduce the difference' recipe is not enough; the recipe must be tied to the problem class or verified step by step. Supports keeping O5 as a checked operator, not a prompt slogan.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (Apple)
finding: Reasoning models show accuracy collapse on Tower of Hanoi, Checkers Jumping, River Crossing and Blocks World beyond a complexity threshold. Reasoning effort falls near the collapse point. Giving the explicit recursive Hanoi algorithm did not move the collapse point.
numbers: Models: o3-mini (medium, high), DeepSeek-R1, R1-Qwen-32B, Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking. Three regimes: non-thinking better at low complexity, thinking better at medium, both zero at high. Claude 3.7 near-perfect at Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) but fails River Crossing N=3 (11 moves); first error near move 100 at Hanoi N=10 vs move 4 in River Crossing.
limits: Contested: see b06. Evaluation required full move lists, so output length is a confound.
agent_relevance: Even a handed-over subgoal recursion is executed unreliably over long chains. Execute in small verified steps.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Much of the Hanoi collapse is a token-limit and scoring artifact. Some River Crossing instances (N>=6 with boat capacity 3) are mathematically impossible yet scored as failures. Asking for a program instead of a move list restored high accuracy.
numbers: Hanoi needs 2^N-1 moves; at 10 tokens per move the 64k-token limit caps solvable size near N=12-13, but reported collapse is near N=9, so models also stop early. Lua generator for N=15: very high accuracy in Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5, under 5,000 tokens (preliminary, no table).
quote: apparent reasoning failures reflect constraints on solution length rather than fundamental reasoning limitations
limits: Short note, preliminary experiments, no full numbers. Author used an LLM as co-writer; a first version had an error that commenters caught.
agent_relevance: Separate 'knows the subgoal structure' from 'can emit every step'. Let the agent write and run a small program for the mechanical part.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER)
finding: Extreme decomposition into single-step microagents plus per-step voting (first-to-ahead-by-k) solved 20-disk Towers of Hanoi (over one million steps) with zero errors using a small base model.
numbers: 20 disks = 2^20-1 steps. gpt-4.1-mini, max 750 output tokens, k_min=3, red-flag parser, temperature 0 first sample then 0.1. Expected cost grows as s ln s with step count s. Projected cost table: gpt-4.1-mini about $3.5K; haiku-4.5 about $71.2K.
limits: The decomposition (what one step is) was given in advance; the paper says automatic discovery of decompositions is open. Hanoi has a known recursive strategy.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that error control per step, not a smarter model, scales a goal-subgoal loop. Fits a verify-each-subgoal rule in O5.

source: Webb, Mondal, Momennejad (2025) Modular Agentic Planner (MAP), Nature Communications 16:8633
finding: Splitting planning into LLM modules including a TaskDecomposer (subgoal generator), actor, monitor and tree search beats ToT, CoT, ICL and debate on Tower of Hanoi, CogEval graph traversal and PlanBench. Ablations show subgoals and the monitor matter.
numbers: Hanoi 3-disk (text digit-list version): GPT-4 zero-shot 11%, MAP 74% (every problem solved at least once in 5 runs). 4-disk out of distribution: MAP 24%, best baseline GPT-4 CoT 5%. Ablation: MAP 74, with 2 subgoals 82, without TaskDecomposer 50, without tree search 32, without Monitor 27 (invalid moves 31%). Llama3-70B: MAP 50% vs CoT 29.2%. PlanBench Logistics: MAP 24 vs CoT 17; Mystery BW: MAP 27.4 vs CoT 10.6. Logistics with vs without TaskDecomposer: 24% vs 20.5%.
limits: Higher compute cost than plain prompting. Hanoi 4-disk MAP is a single run. Gains from subgoals alone are modest on PlanBench (24 vs 20.5).
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of a difference-reduction loop in an LLM: subgoal generation helps (74 vs 50), a monitor that rejects invalid moves helps more (74 vs 27). Keep a state checker in the loop.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Search over partial 'thoughts' with self-evaluation and lookahead beats chain-of-thought on Game of 24. Most CoT failures happen at the first step.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, IO+refine 27%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Oracle best-of-100: IO 33%, CoT 49%. About 60% of CoT samples fail after the first step.
limits: Search over the next state, not strict means-ends analysis. Three tasks only; compute cost is higher.
agent_relevance: Choosing the first step wrongly kills the run. Evaluate several candidate subgoals before committing (supports a branching step at O5).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting, ICLR
finding: Explicit decomposition into ordered subproblems with each answer feeding the next generalises to harder instances than CoT on symbolic and compositional tasks. Gains on math word problems are small.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, CoT 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%. Last-letter concatenation, length 12: CoT 31.8% (37.4-38.4% with extra exemplars) vs least-to-most 74.0%. GSM8K overall: CoT 60.87 (text says 60.97) vs 62.39; problems needing 5 or more steps: 39.07 vs 45.23.
limits: Effect is large when subproblems are well defined and independent; near zero on GSM8K as a whole. Code model with strong exemplars.
agent_relevance: Decomposition pays most at the hard end (5+ steps), so trigger explicit subgoals by estimated depth, not always.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner
finding: Language agents fail at multi-constraint real-world planning, with GPT-4 almost never producing a fully valid plan.
numbers: 1,225 planning intents; GPT-4 final pass rate 0.6%; other LLMs 0%.
limits: Abstract and introduction read only. Constraint-heavy, not pure state-goal difference reduction.
agent_relevance: When many constraints interact, local difference reduction loses track of them; keep an explicit constraint ledger.

source: Loconte et al. (2024) Challenging LLMs' intelligence with human neuropsychological tests, Heliyon
finding: On a text version of the Tower of London (a goal-subgoal planning test), all tested LLMs scored severely impaired relative to human norms even with a one-shot chain-of-thought example, while scoring normal on most other prefrontal tests.
numbers: ToL raw score out of 36: GPT-3.5 7, GPT-4 8, Claude2 2, Llama2 0; GPT-3.5 below the first percentile of human norms. GPT-4 within norms on every task except planning. Failures: rule-violating moves and wrong description of the reached state.
limits: Text adaptation of ToL (Italian), one-shot prompt, 2023 models. Spatial-state tracking is a confound.
agent_relevance: Planning is the weak spot even when verbal tests are normal; the failure is state tracking, which a scaffold should hand to an explicit state record.

source: Donnarumma, Maisto, Pezzulo (2016) Problem solving as probabilistic inference with subgoaling, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: A model that uses subgoals as waypoints reproduces two human Tower of Hanoi quirks: preference for paths that stay inside one cluster of the state graph, and difficulty with counterintuitive moves that go away from the goal. A perceptual 'put disks on the goal rod' strategy is modelled as a different prior, not a different mechanism.
numbers: Cited human data: when two shortest Hanoi paths exist (one crossing one bottleneck, one crossing two), participants chose the one-bottleneck path in 72% of cases.
limits: Simulation paper; the 72% is a result it cites from earlier experiments, not one it ran. Three-disk Hanoi only.
agent_relevance: Pure difference reduction fails at moves that raise the difference. The scaffold needs a rule for 'step back to move forward' (temporarily widen the gap) at O5.

source: Eluchans et al. (2025) Adaptive planning depth in human problem-solving, Royal Society Open Science
finding: People choose an initial plan depth that matches the minimum number of subgoals the problem needs, not one fixed depth. This fits bounded rationality: spend search where the problem needs it.
numbers: Problems needing 1 to 8 subgoals; compared participants to planning models (sample size not recorded in the part read).
limits: Abstract and introduction read; sample size and effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Match lookahead depth to estimated subgoal count; do not use one fixed depth (links to the metareasoning subfield).

source: Correa et al. (2023) Humans decompose tasks by trading off utility and computational cost, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: People pick subgoals that cut planning cost while keeping performance; their choices fit a betweenness-centrality heuristic better than two other normative accounts.
numbers: N = 806 participants; 30 random graphs; model analysis over 11,117 graph tasks.
limits: Graph-navigation tasks, not Hanoi-style move puzzles. Abstract level read.
agent_relevance: Pick subgoals at bottlenecks (high betweenness) in the state graph. A usable rule for subgoal choice in O5.

source: Does difficulty moderate learning? Desirable difficulties vs cognitive load theory (2025)
finding: Cognitive load theory holds that, for novices without a schema, means-ends analysis is working-memory heavy and does not build schemas. The goal-free and worked-example effects are the two proposed fixes. The review lists supporting studies but gives no new effect sizes.
numbers: Cited support for goal-free effect: Ayres 1993 (Contemp Educ Psychol 18:376), Bobis et al. 1994, Owen and Sweller 1985, Vollmeyer et al. 1996. No pooled effect size in the page.
limits: Secondary source. I could not verify which citing studies show null results.
agent_relevance: Keep two uses of MEA apart: MEA as a way to solve (works) and as a way to learn (poor). The agent has no schema-building need within one task, so the CLT objection matters less, but MEA is the fallback when no stored pattern matches.

source: Cognitive load theory restatement of MEA (Biological evolution and human cognition are analogous information processing systems, 2023)
finding: States MEA as: consider current state, goal state, differences, and a move that reduces them; common when few moves are available; argues the strategy needs no teaching, while a worked example removes the load.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Theory statement, not data. CLT authors treat general strategies as biologically primary (evolved).
agent_relevance: Gives the plain definition to put in the scaffold: state, goal, difference, operator.

source: Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System (2025)
finding: Notes the debate on whether MEA needs explicit teaching: cognitive load theory says no (primary skill), others suggest worked examples of applying MEA help beginners. Courses teach cross-domain methods built on MEA (Newell and Simon 1972, Polya 1945).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Position paper; the claim that MEA is not teachable is not backed by a cited experiment in the page.
agent_relevance: Open question whether instruction helps; for an LLM, 'teaching' means prompt design, and b04 suggests specific demonstrations beat general ones.

source: Effects of example-free instruction and worked examples on problem-solving (Heliyon, 2021)
finding: Small study: explanation without examples beat worked examples without explanation for critical-thinking problems. Mentions that background explanation can reduce wasteful means-ends or trial-and-error search.
numbers: n = 32 university students in South Korea.
limits: Very small sample; critical-thinking items, not state-goal puzzles. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Low weight. Shows that the worked-example advantage is not universal.

source: Meta-analysis: effect of the Means Ends Analysis (MEA) learning model on students' mathematical problem-solving (Desimal, 2023)
finding: An Indonesian meta-analysis of a classroom 'MEA learning model' reports a very large pooled effect on math problem solving.
numbers: Pooled effect size 1.431 (Cohen formula, SPSS). Number of studies not seen. Junior high effect described as large.
limits: Abstract only via Crossref; full text blocked (403). Different construct from Newell-Simon MEA (a teaching format). Likely small local studies with publication bias. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Do not use as evidence for the search method. Warn readers about the name collision.

source: Meta-analysis: effect of Means Ends Analysis (MEA) model on mathematical problem-solving skills (Edumaspul, 2023)
finding: A second Indonesian meta-analysis of the same classroom model gives a smaller but still large pooled effect, and no moderation by education level or demographics.
numbers: 18 articles (2009-2023), random-effects model (CMA); overall effect size 0.920.
limits: Abstract only. Same construct problem as b20. Study quality and bias tests not seen.
agent_relevance: Same caution. Two meta-analyses disagree by about 0.5 SD (1.431 vs 0.920), which shows how unstable this literature is.

source: Sweller and Levine (1982) Effects of goal specificity on means-ends analysis and learning, JEP: LMC 8(5):463
finding: Founding goal-specificity experiments (maze tasks): subjects with a specific goal use means-ends analysis and learn less about the problem structure than subjects without a specific goal. Record confirmed via Crossref (93 citations); content is from memory.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Core human result behind the 'MEA solves but does not teach' claim.

source: Sweller, Mawer, Ward (1983) Development of expertise in mathematical problem solving, JEP: General 112:639
finding: Experts work forward from givens; novices use means-ends analysis working backward from the goal. Reported as the basis for the claim that MEA is a novice strategy.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Direction of the effect depends on domain and problem type.
agent_relevance: In the agent, forward chaining from known facts is the expert mode and difference reduction is the fallback. Order the choice by whether a stored pattern matches.

source: Owen and Sweller (1985) J Educ Psychol 77:272; Ayres (1993) Why goal-free problems can facilitate learning, Contemp Educ Psychol 18:376
finding: Goal-free problems ('find as many values as you can') improved learning in geometry and trigonometry; Ayres replicated and gave an account in terms of reduced search load. Ayres 1993 details confirmed from a reference list in b16.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Possible boundary (to verify): the effect appears for problems where MEA is the default strategy and many moves are possible; weaker for low-interactivity or familiar problems.
agent_relevance: Goal-free exploration is a legitimate alternative to O5 when the aim is to learn the structure of a new domain, not to reach a goal fast.

source: Vollmeyer, Burns, Holyoak (1996) The impact of goal specificity on strategy use and the acquisition of problem structure, Cognitive Science 20:75
finding: With a complex system, a non-specific goal group tested hypotheses more systematically and learned the system's structure better than a specific-goal group. A specific goal helped when the system was simple.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Burns and Vollmeyer (2002, QJEP 55A:241) is the follow-up on goal specificity and hypothesis testing; the specific-goal cost is reported to depend on system complexity.
agent_relevance: Complexity moderates: use plain difference reduction on simple goals, switch to exploratory or goal-free probing on complex hidden-structure problems.

source: Simon (1975) The functional equivalence of problem solving skills, Cognitive Psychology 7:268; Anzai and Simon (1979) The theory of learning by doing, Psychol Rev 86:124
finding: Tower of Hanoi can be solved by several distinct strategies (goal-recursion, perceptual, move-pattern). One subject followed over five attempts shifted from means-ends search to a goal-recursive strategy, with fewer moves.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Single-subject learning study in Anzai and Simon (1979).
agent_relevance: Strategy is a variable, not fixed: the scaffold should log which strategy was used on each subgoal.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes, Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi, Cognitive Psychology 17:248
finding: Isomorphs of Hanoi that differ only in how moves are described (move vs change rules) differ greatly in difficulty. The explanation is that difficulty comes from the rules' load on working memory and perceptual cues, not the abstract search space. Zhang and Norman (1994, Cognitive Science 18:87) later showed external representation of the rules changes difficulty.
numbers: I recall difficulty ratios of up to about sixteen between isomorphs; not verified.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Problem representation, not abstract structure, sets difficulty. Reformulate a hard-looking goal into an easier isomorphic form before reducing differences.

source: Thomas (1974) An analysis of behavior in the hobbits-orcs problem, Cognitive Psychology 6:257; Jeffries, Polson, Razran, Atwood (1977) A process model for missionaries-cannibals
finding: In river-crossing puzzles, participants stall at the step where the correct move increases the apparent distance to the goal (moving people back). Difference-reduction models predict this stall.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Same failure shape as the counterintuitive move in b13 and Goel and Grafman (1995) on frontal patients. Needs an explicit 'allowed to regress' operator.

source: Goel and Grafman (1995) Are the frontal lobes implicated in planning functions? Interpreting data from the Tower of Hanoi, Neuropsychologia 33:623
finding: Frontal-lobe patients were mainly impaired on the counterintuitive move that must go against the goal-reduction heuristic, suggesting a limit in suspending goal-driven difference reduction rather than in planning in general.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Small clinical sample; later literature disputes how specific the Hanoi deficit is to prefrontal damage.
agent_relevance: Supports adding an override for subgoal conflicts.

source: Sussman anomaly and non-serializable subgoals (Sussman 1973; Chapman 1987 Planning for conjunctive goals, AI 32:333; Korf 1987 Planning as search, AI 33:65)
finding: Linear means-ends planners that achieve one goal at a time and never undo it fail on tasks whose subgoals interact (the three-block Sussman anomaly). Korf: subgoals are serializable only for some domains; Rubik's-cube-style puzzles are not. Complete partial-order planning (Chapman) removes the failure.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session (paywalled). Recalled from the literature; verify before citing. Modern heuristic planners (delete-relaxation, landmark) generalise difference reduction and are the working baseline in b03: Fast Downward solves 600/600 Blocksworld.
agent_relevance: Main theoretical boundary for O5: do not lock a finished subgoal. Re-check earlier subgoals after each step.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Position paper: autoregressive LLMs cannot by themselves plan or self-verify; they work as approximate knowledge sources inside loops with external verifiers.
numbers: No numbers read on this page. The o1 paper (b03) quotes 82% on a Blocksworld subset and 70% on Logistics for LLM-Modulo.
limits: Abstract page only; position paper.
agent_relevance: Design rule: LLM proposes the subgoal or operator, external check accepts it.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) Planning in Strawberry Fields: o1 on planning and scheduling
finding: o1 improves planning over earlier LLMs at high inference cost and still gives no correctness guarantees; adding an external verifier (LRM-Modulo) guarantees correctness and improves results.
numbers: No numbers read on this page.
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Verifier in the loop beats a bigger reasoner alone.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong
finding: Iterative self-critique on graph colouring does not help GPT-4, which is poor at verifying its own answers; external correct verification does help.
numbers: No numbers read on this page.
limits: Abstract page only. Graph colouring, not state-goal planning.
agent_relevance: Progress check ('did the difference shrink?') must come from a tool or a rule, not the model's own judgment.
